name: Uptime with excused outages
brief:
A status page logs one letter per day for a pricing service: `U` when it was up and `D` when it was down. The supplier may excuse at most `k` down days in a reported run. The input comes as one string:

- the first line holds `n` and `k`, separated by a space;
- the second line holds the `n` letters with no spaces between them (it may be missing when `n` is 0).

Write `solve_excused_outages(text)`, which returns, as a string, the length of the longest run of consecutive days holding at most `k` down days. Expect extra spaces and a trailing newline.

Example. For `"7 1\nUUDUUDU\n"` the first five days hold one `D`, and so do the last four. The answer is `"5"`.
constraints: $O(n)$ time is the target. Trying every start and end is too slow.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Read the tokens with `text.split()`. Grow a window one day at a time, and while it holds more than `k` down days, move its left edge on.

examples.note: Either run of five days holds one outage; any run of six holds two.
No outage may be excused and every day was down, so no run counts.

how: Submit runs 14 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value.
notes: The window always holds the longest run ending today with at most `k` down days.
The longest run of up days plus `k` is not the answer: the excused days must sit inside one run.
Each day enters the window once and leaves at most once, so the work is $O(n)$.

planted.slip: Adding `k` to the longest up run assumes the excused days sit next to it, which they need not.
Reading the second line raw keeps its spaces, which then count as down days.
Starting a new run at today when the excuses run out throws away the days that could still be kept.
